claims.text: Uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding undergoes rapid, exothermic oxidation at high temperatures.
High-temperature oxidation of uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding generates hydrogen.
A 2–5 μm MoSi2 coating can be applied to zirconium-alloy cladding by chemical vapor deposition.
A 2–5 μm MoSi2 coating will improve the high-temperature oxidation resistance of zirconium-alloy cladding relative to uncoated cladding.
The MoSi2 coating remains chemically inert at normal reactor operating temperatures of approximately 300–400°C.
The MoSi2 coating becomes oxidation-active during steam exposure at approximately 1200–1300°C.
At high temperature, the MoSi2 coating forms an adherent, slow-growing SiO2-rich layer.
Oxidation of the MoSi2 coating leaves a Mo-containing interlayer beneath the SiO2-rich layer.
The SiO2-rich scale and Mo-containing interlayer act as a barrier to oxygen transport.
Preferential oxidation of MoSi2 produces a dense SiO2-rich scale during a high-temperature transient.
The SiO2-rich barrier impedes oxygen diffusion to the underlying zirconium alloy.
Reduced oxygen transport to the zirconium alloy slows its rapid exothermic oxidation.
Slower oxidation of the zirconium alloy reduces hydrogen generation.
The thin coating preserves cladding mechanical integrity during normal operation.
The thin coating has negligible impact on neutron economy during normal operation.
Compared with uncoated cladding, coated cladding will show significantly reduced oxidation kinetics during 1200–1300°C steam transients.
Compared with uncoated cladding, coated cladding will generate less hydrogen during 1200–1300°C steam transients.
The coating will preserve the cladding's mechanical and thermal properties under normal reactor conditions.
The coating will preserve neutron-transparent behavior under normal reactor conditions.
The oxidation benefit depends on the coating avoiding adhesion failure, spallation, and harmful thermal-expansion mismatch during steam exposure and thermal cycling.
